content: The objective of the FLORIDA trial was to evaluate the impact of fluvastatin on residual ischemia following an acute myocardial infarction. The FLORIDA trial, which stands for Fluvastatin On Risk Diminishment after Acute myocardial infarction, was a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blinded, parallel study. It included 540 patients who had experienced an acute myocardial infarction and had serum cholesterol levels below 251 mg/dL. The study utilized ambulatory electrocardiographic (AECG) monitoring to assess ischemia at three time points: baseline, after six weeks, and at 12 months. Patients were randomly assigned to receive either fluvastatin or a placebo. At the 12-month mark, the fluvastatin treatment group demonstrated a 13% reduction in serum total cholesterol (TC) levels and a 21% reduction in LDL-C levels. In contrast, the placebo group exhibited a 9% increase in total cholesterol levels. Baseline AECG monitoring revealed ischemia in 11% of the patients. After six weeks, 67% (32 out of 48) of the patients who had ischemia at baseline no longer showed signs of ischemia. By 12 months, this percentage increased to 76% (35 out of 46). In conclusion, fluvastatin treatment, when compared to placebo, did not have a significant effect on ischemia as measured by AECG or on the occurrence of major clinical events.
